text: Every chapter in this course is a layer in the same program, and this capstone is where they stop being seven separate topics and start being one system. Prevention keeps bad traffic and known weaknesses out before detection has to catch anything, detection catches what prevention missed, and response is what happens once something is actually caught — Lessons 29 through 31 showed exactly what that looks like applied to one real company.

Chapter 1 covered stateful and next-generation firewalls, DMZ design, and VLAN segmentation, which Lesson 29's lab put directly into practice. Chapters 2 and 3 covered IDS and IPS, Suricata rule syntax, and NetFlow baselining, which Lessons 30 and 31 turned into working rules and the first signal in a real case. Chapter 4 covered EDR telemetry, process trees, and containment.

Chapter 5 covered threat intelligence, IOCs, and STIX and TAXII, which supplied the second signal in Lesson 31's case study. Chapter 6 covered vulnerability scanners and the vulnerability management lifecycle, the other half of the prevention layer alongside Chapter 1. Chapter 7 covered honeypots and deception, detection that works because no legitimate user ever has a reason to touch one.

Lesson 31's exfiltration is the clearest proof this has to be layered. The firewall rules from Chapter 1 didn't stop it, because the traffic looked like ordinary outbound HTTPS. It took a flow baseline from Chapter 3, a threat intel match from Chapter 5, and EDR telemetry from Chapter 4 together to catch what any one layer alone would have missed.

That's the full course: from a single stateful firewall rule to a layered program that segments a network, writes its own detection rules, reads its own traffic baselines, acts on threat intelligence, scans for and tracks its own weaknesses, deploys deception to catch what else slips through, and responds to what its endpoints catch. Course complete. Next up in this path: SOC Operations, SIEM & Log Analysis.
